paper_title: Future Representation Distillation for Imagination-free World Action Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: World Action Models (WAMs) use the predictive knowledge of pretrained video diffusion models for robot control through future video prediction. However, iterative video denoising is costly, and inaccurate visual predictions can compromise action prediction. Our key idea is to make this predictive knowledge available through visual representations computed from the current observation, enabling action prediction without generating future videos. We introduce DreamFree, a WAM that repurposes a pretrained video diffusion model as a predictive visual encoder through representation distillation. The visual encoder learns to predict a frozen video diffusion model's representation using only the current observation. An action module is then trained to predict actions by extracting action-relevant information from the visual encoder. Across real-world and simulated tasks, DreamFree achieves higher success rates than state-of-the-art VLAs and WAMs, while performing real-time closed-loop control at 11Hz with a 14B video diffusion backbone. Experiments show that DreamFree can translate stronger video priors and additional video data into better robot control and enable learning new robot tasks from video demonstrations, including videos from a different embodiment, without action annotation for the new tasks.

A MF distills predictive knowledge from frozen video diffusion model into predictive visual encoder, enabling action prediction from the current observation without generating future videos. In real-world evaluations, A MF achieves higher success than DreamZero and 𝜋0.5 with latency comparable to that of 𝜋0.5 and 17.8 inference speedup over DreamZero. A MF generalizes across diverse real-world manipulation tasks. 1. Introduction Pretrained video diffusion models offer promising foundation for robot control [35, 15, 9]. Through large-scale video pretraining, these models learn to predict how physical environments evolve over time, providing predictive knowledge that can guide robot actions. World Action Models (WAMs; Ye et al. [28]) use this knowledge by adapting video models to predict visual futures and actions, demonstrating strong manipulation performance and generalization to new tasks and environments [15, 28]. common approach in WAMs is to use this predictive knowledge of pretrained video diffusion models through future video prediction, either by jointly predicting visual futures and actions [15, 28] or by decoding actions from predicted visual futures [10, 21]. These methods leverage the pretrained models knowledge through their native video prediction process. However, iterative video denoising incurs substantial inference cost, and errors in the predicted visual futures can lead to inaccurate actions. Moreover, it remains unclear whether action prediction requires the same level of visual detail as video generation. central question is how to make better use of the predictive knowledge in pretrained video models for action prediction. The success of video-generating WAMs demonstrates the value of this knowledge, while leaving open how it should be represented to support control. This motivates investigating whether predictive information can be made directly available in the visual features used for action prediction. We hypothesize that this predictive knowledge can be effectively captured in visual representations to support action prediction, without iterative video denoising. Our key idea is to distill the video models predictive knowledge into the visual representations computed from the current observation. We train visual encoder to anticipate visual futures from the observation by using the representations extracted from pretrained video diffusion model. Our analysis shows that distillation enables the encoder to effectively capture future visual information from the current observation and make its features more useful for action prediction. The resulting predictive representations enable action prediction without generating future videos. Based on this finding, we introduce A MF E, WAM that repurposes pretrained video diffusion backbone as predictive visual encoder through representation distillation. We train the model in two stages, separating predictive representation learning from action learning. In the first stage, frozen video diffusion model extracts representations from both current and future frames of video demonstration, and the visual encoder learns to predict these representations from the current observation. The encoder thus learns to anticipate scene evolution in feature space, making the video models predictive knowledge available in single forward pass without future video generation. This stage requires no action labels, allowing the visual encoder to learn from any in-the-wild video demonstrations. In the second stage, we train an action module on robot demonstrations to map these visual features to executable actions, with the visual encoder either frozen or jointly fine-tuned. 3 We evaluate A MF on diverse manipulation tasks in both simulation and real-world environments [12], demonstrating stronger performance compared to state-of-the-art VLA and WAM baselines [23, 28]. In real-world evaluations, A MF succeeds on tasks involving object deformation or successive rearrangements where video-generating WAM fails (Figure 1). These successes suggest benefit of using predictive visual representations for control without relying on potentially inaccurate video predictions. Experiments show that using larger video backbone and additional pretraining video data improve success, demonstrating A MF can translate stronger video priors and additional video data into better robot control without additional action annotation. We additionally show task transfer from video demonstrations, including videos from different embodiment, showing that A MF can learn new tasks from videos without collecting action annotations for those tasks. In addition to strong performance, A MF offers practical advantage for real-time control. During deployment, the policy obtains predictive visual representations in single encoder pass and uses them to generate an action chunk without iterative video denoising. A MF using 14B video backbone achieves real-time closed-loop control at 11Hz, achieving 17.8 inference speedup over video-generating WAM with the same video backbone size and latency comparable to that of VLA (Figure 1, middle). We highlight our main contributions below: We introduce A MF E, WAM that repurposes pretrained video diffusion backbone as predictive visual encoder by distilling future information from frozen video diffusion model. We outperform state-of-the-art VLA and WAM baselines in real-world manipulation without taskspecific adaptation, while achieving real-time closed-loop control at 11Hz. We show that A MF translates stronger video priors and additional video data into better robot control. We demonstrate that A MF can learn new tasks from video demonstrations, including videos from different embodiment, without action annotations for the new tasks. 2. Related work Vision-language-action policies Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies adapt pretrained visionlanguage models to map visual observations and language instructions directly to robot actions [23, 6, 36, 5, 13]. While their backbones provide semantic and linguistic priors, pretraining on static image-text pairs gives them limited knowledge of the spatiotemporal dynamics important for robot control. Video model-based robot policies Video model-based robot policies build on pretrained video diffusion models by coupling future visual prediction with action prediction. Some decode actions from video representations through inverse dynamics [10, 21, 24], while others jointly denoise future video and action sequences [15, 16, 4, 18, 28]. These World Action Models (WAMs) transfer spatiotemporal video priors to control, achieving strong action-data efficiency and generalization. However, generating future video at deployment introduces substantial inference cost, and errors in the predicted video can lead to inaccurate action prediction. Recent works retain video prediction during training while enabling action prediction without future video generation at deployment [30, 27], yet how faithfully their representations preserve the video models predictive knowledge remains unclear. Predictive visual representation learning Predictive visual learning methods train encoders to capture scene structure and dynamics by predicting representations of unobserved visual content [2]. Related predictive supervision is used in VLA policies, where future images or visual features serve as auxiliary training targets alongside action supervision [26, 33, 32]. For example, FLARE [34] aligns future tokens in the action expert with vision-language embeddings of future observations. Our approach learns predictive visual representations from the current observation by distilling features from frozen video diffusion model into visual encoder. Figure 2 Model architecture of A MF E. Training is separated into two stages: (a) In the first stage, pretrained video diffusion backbone is repurposed as visual encoder through video generative training with structured attention mask and distillation of predictive representations from the frozen video diffusion model. (b) In the second stage, the action readout module and action decoder are trained to predict actions by extracting action-relevant information from the encoder. 3. A E As shown in Figure 2, A MF consists of predictive visual encoder followed by an action module. The training stage of A MF is separated into two stages. First, the predictive visual encoder is trained to predict the representations from the frozen video diffusion model (Section 3.1). The frozen video diffusion model extracts representations from both current and future frames of video demonstration, while the visual encoder conditions on the current observation only. Second, the action module is trained to predict actions by extracting action-relevant information from the predictive visual encoder through readout module (Section 3.2). During inference, only single forward pass through the predictive visual encoder is required to extract visual features relevant for action prediction, enabling real-time closed-loop control up to 11Hz. 3.1. Learning predictive visual encoder Predictive visual encoder We initialize the encoder from pretrained video diffusion backbone and use the hidden states of its current-frame latent tokens as the visual representation. We apply structured mask to the backbones bidirectional video self-attention (Figure 2(a) left), restricting current-frame tokens to attend only to each other within self-attention. This ensures that the current-frame hidden states depend only on the current observation and instruction. During training, the backbone receives clean current frame and noisy future frames, as shown in Figure 2(a). Future representation distillation The main idea is to distill the representation of frozen video diffusion model into the visual encoder that observes only the current observation and instruction. Motivated by REPA [29], we introduce future representation distillation, which aligns the projection of the encoders current frame representation with video diffusion model representation as shown in Figure 2(a). Learning actions from visual representations After training the predictive visual encoder, we use action-labeled robot demonstrations to train the action module, which consists of readout module, state and action encoders, and an action decoder. Given the observation and instruction, the visual encoder produces the predictive representation that serves as visual prior for the action module. Then the readout module extracts action-relevant features from the representation, and the action module conditions on the action-relevant features together with the instruction and proprioception to predict the action chunk, as illustrated in Figure 2(b). We transform these visual tokens into fixed number of action-facing tokens using latent-query readout inspired by Perceiver [11]. Inference Without Iterative Video Denoising During inference, the predictive visual encoder processes the observation and instruction in single forward pass. The resulting predictive visual representation is transformed by the readout into action-facing tokens, and the action decoder conditions on these to generate an action chunk using 𝑁 denoising steps. This enables real-time closed-loop control up to 11Hz even for 14B video backbone. 4. Experiments We validate the performance of A MF in both simulation and real-world environments. In particular, we investigate the following questions: (Q1) Does distillation make visual features more useful for action prediction? (Q2) Do representations learned by A MF translate into strong manipulation performance? (Q3) Can A MF translate stronger video priors and additional video data into better control? (Q4) How effectively and efficiently does A MF perform real-world manipulation? (Q5) Can A MF learn new tasks from video demonstrations without action annotations? 6 Figure 3 Representation analysis. We evaluate visual representations by measuring how accurately action sequences (Action probing) and future-frame VAE latents (Future probing) can be decoded from them. Future representation distillation makes the encoders features more useful for action prediction and improves their ability to capture future visual information from the current observation. 4.1. Experimental setup Implementation details We use pretrained Wan2.2-5B and Wan2.2-A14B high-noise expert [25] as the video backbone, including the video DiT, text encoder, and video VAE. The action decoder is 1B DiT. For all experiments, we set the action horizon to 32. Following Fast-WAM [30], we temporally downsample the videos by 4, producing 9 video frames per chunk. A MF is trained on each dataset without cross-embodiment pretraining. We provide more details in Appendix A. Benchmarks We evaluate our method on two simulation benchmarks and one real-world evaluation setup. For LIBERO [17], we follow the standard benchmarking protocol, using four task suites (Spatial, Object, Goal, Long). For RoboCasa-Kitchen [19], we follow the 24-task benchmark protocol of Kim et al. [15] and train on their released dataset, which contains 50 demos per task. The tasks span object placement and manipulation of kitchen fixtures and appliances. For real-world evaluation, we use the DROID [12] setup, evaluating on 10 tasks selected from the pretraining distribution spanning diverse capabilities, including push, cover, press, fold, pour, and composite skills (see Appendix C.2). We measure the task progress and success rate using 5 rollouts per task. We provide task descriptions and evaluation details in Appendix C.2. Baselines On simulation benchmarks, we compare A MF against state-of-the-art VLAs [6, 23, 14, 5, 34] and WAMs [4, 16, 30, 15]. For real-world DROID evaluation, we compare with state-of-the-art VLA 𝜋0.5 and WAM DreamZero [28] with their publicly released checkpoints, namely 𝜋0.5-DROID and DreamZero-DROID, following their inference setup. 4.2. Q1: Representation analysis We examine whether future representation distillation makes the visual encoders representation more useful for action prediction. We compare features from three models given only the current observation: the pretrained video diffusion model (VDM), variant of the A MF visual encoder trained without distillation, and the visual encoder of A MF E. As reference with direct access to future observations, we also evaluate VDM representations computed from both the current frame and groundtruth future frames. The VDM and encoders use the 14B video backbone and are conditioned on the language instructions. Each encoder is trained separately on Robocasa-Kitchen and DROID datasets. For each representation and input setting, we train separate probe while keeping the feature extractor frozen. We report normalized mean squared error in Figure 3. Action probing To assess the usefulness of the features for control, we train lightweight attentionbased probe to predict action sequences from each representation, using paired robot demonstration videos and actions. As an additional reference, we also probe VAE latents of both the current and ground-truth future frames to compare the encoder representations with direct encodings of future observations. Figure 3 shows that the A MF encoder achieves lower action prediction error than the VDM using only the current observation and the encoder variant trained without distillation. Future probing To better understand the improvement in action decodability from distillation, we examine whether distillation improves the encoders ability to capture future visual information from the current observation. We train spatially shared linear probe to reconstruct the VAE latent patches of ground-truth future frames. Figure 3 shows that A MF encoder achieves lower reconstruction error than the VDM using only the current observation and the encoder variant trained without distillation. Furthermore, its reconstruction error approaches that of the VDM given future frames on RoboCasa-Kitchen, while gap remains on DROID. These results show that our encoder effectively captures future visual information from the current observation. 4.3. Q2 & Q3: Performance and scaling on simulation benchmarks We first assess in-distribution task execution of A MF in the LIBERO benchmark compared to VLAs and WAMs. In Table 1, A MF achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art baselines even without cross-embodiment pretraining, supporting the effectiveness of A MF Es predictive visual representations for in-distribution manipulation. We next evaluate A MF on the RoboCasa-Kitchen benchmark to assess multi-task manipulation under object and scene variation, with limited demonstration data. Table 2 shows that A MF with 14B video backbone achieves the highest average success rate of 71.7%, demonstrating that our predictive visual representations can translate pretrained video knowledge into strong manipulation performance without generating future videos. Fast-WAM also predicts actions without generating future videos at inference, but underperforms the other baselines with only 44.4% success, suggesting that using video priors without future video generation remains challenging in this setting. Moreover, we investigate whether A MF benefits from larger video backbone and more pretraining video data. Fast-WAM shows little improvement when its backbone is scaled from 5B to 14B, suggesting limited benefit from stronger video priors. In contrast, scaling our video backbone from 5B to 14B improves success rate by 13.2 pp, with particularly large gains on pick-and-place tasks. These gains suggest that stronger video priors provide more useful representations for coordinating grasping, transport, and placement. We also use videos from the atomic-task subset of RoboCasa365 [20] showing robot demonstrations in simulated kitchen environments. Training the visual encoder with these videos, without their action labels, further improves success. Together, these results show that A MF can translate stronger video priors and additional video data into better robot control, without additional action annotations. 8 Figure 4 Real-world evaluation on DROID. We evaluate policies out of the box on 10 tasks with five trials per task. Task descriptions and the progress scoring criteria are provided in Appendix C.2. To assess how each visual encoder training objective contributes to performance, we ablate the generative objective Lgen and distillation objective Ldistill. As shown in Table 3, removing the distillation objective Ldistill leads to significant drop in the success rate for both datasets. Removing the generative objective Lgen also degrades the performance, although the drops are smaller compared to removing the distillation objective. These results indicate that both objectives contribute to learning predictive visual representations, with distillation playing particularly important role in translating pretrained video knowledge into strong manipulation performance. Q4: Real-world performance and efficiency Real-world manipulation To assess real-world manipulation and generalization, we evaluate the models out of the box on 10 task types represented in the pretraining data, using new objects or scene arrangements. Figure 4 reports the task progress and success rates. A MF achieves the highest average success rate at 64%, compared with 56% for DreamZero and 16% for 𝜋0.5, with successful executions spanning broader range of task types than either baseline. A MF also achieves the highest average task progress at 83%, compared with 71.8% for DreamZero and 33.5% for 𝜋0.5. The gains over DreamZero are notable in tasks involving deformable object manipulation or successive rearrangements, such as cover strawberry with towel, hang hat on tripod, and put bolts in bowl. DreamZero fails in all trials for each of these tasks, with inaccurate video predictions observed in most failures. Qualitatively, DreamZero often persists with unsuccessful actions after an initial error, Figure 6 Examples of real-world bimanual manipulation task executions. We show selected frames from successful rollouts of A MF E. whereas A MF often adjusts its actions and recovers. Together with the analysis in Section 4.2, these observations suggest that A MF benefits from capturing predictive information directly in its visual representations, enabling successful control without relying on potentially inaccurate future video predictions. These results demonstrate that A MF achieves effective real-world control and generalizes zero-shot to new objects or scene arrangements within seen tasks. We describe the failure cases of A MF in Appendix D.3. Real-world bimanual manipulation We further examine the applicability of A MF to another real-world embodiment using bimanual YAM setup. We train A MF on filtered 100-hour subset of ABC-130k [1] without additional cross-embodiment training. We deploy the resulting policy out of the box without task adaptation, evaluating tasks represented in the training set but using new scenes, objects, and arrangements. Figure 6 presents successful executions of bimanual manipulation tasks, including pick-and-place, pen uncapping, cloth folding, and dish-rack loading. These qualitative results provide evidence of zero-shot generalization to new scenes and illustrate that our approach can support precise, coordinated two-arm manipulation on physical robot. Q5: Task transfer from video demonstrations We investigate transfer to new tasks using video demonstrations without action annotations. We consider two settings that differ in when target task videos are introduced. In the first setting, the target task videos are introduced during visual encoder pretraining, and we transfer from videos of either the same embodiment or different embodiment. In the second, the target task videos are excluded from initial policy training and introduced for fine-tuning the policy. In both settings, we use only videos of the new tasks without action annotations. Atomic-to-composite task transfer from video pretraining We first investigate whether A MF can learn new composite tasks from videos, using action labels only from atomic tasks. Atomic tasks involve individual skills while composite tasks combine several of these skills sequentially. We compare base A MF trained on atomic tasks in RoboCasa-Kitchen with two variants that additionally use videos of composite tasks for visual encoder training. One variant uses only Lgen without distillation, while the other uses both Lgen and Ldistill. All models use the same action labels from atomic tasks, and the composite tasks are absent from the action-labeled training data. As shown in Figure 8 (left), the base model fails on all tasks, and adding the task videos with distillation raises the average success from 0% to 21.7%, with at least one successful trial on each task. Using the same videos without distillation yields 0% average success. These results demonstrate that A MF can acquire new task knowledge from videos and transfer it to action execution without additional action annotations, with distillation playing an important role in enabling this transfer. Figure 9(a) illustrates successful composite task rollout by A MF E, completing four subgoals in sequence. Cross-embodiment task transfer from video pretraining We next investigate whether A MF can learn new tasks with task videos from different embodiment. We use RoboTwin [7] with ALOHAAgileX as the target robot, and compare base A MF trained on its atomic tasks with variant whose encoder also learns from composite task videos recorded with dual-arm Franka Panda setup. Both models use the same ALOHA-AgileX action labels, and the composite tasks are absent from the action-labeled training. Figure 8 (middle) shows that the base model succeeds only in bowl stacking, with 6.7% average success across the new tasks, and adding task videos from different embodiment improves the average success to 30%. This demonstrates that A MF can transfer task knowledge from different embodiments 11 videos to action execution. Figure 9(b) illustrates successful task rollout by A MF after learning from videos of different embodiment, without access to action-labeled demonstrations of that task. Task adaptation after policy training Finally, we investigate whether target task knowledge can be added after policy training. We start from A MF trained on atomic tasks in RoboTwin, with target tasks excluded from the training set. We then fine-tune only the visual encoder separately for each task using 10 video demonstrations, keeping the action module frozen. Adaptation takes approximately 10 minutes per task on single H200 GPU. We compare demonstrations containing multiple camera views with demonstrations containing only the head camera view. Figure 8 (right) shows that both single-view and multi-view video fine-tuning improve success rates on both tasks, with larger gains from multi-view videos. This shows that task knowledge acquired through video-only fine-tuning of the encoder can transfer to action execution without updating the action module, even with single-camera demonstrations. Figure 9 illustrates successful task rollout with the fine-tuned policy. We find that not all tasks can be learned through video demonstrations. For example, policy unable to open cabinets also failed to learn to place an object inside cabinet through video-only fine-tuning. This suggests that learning new tasks from videos may be limited by the policys ability to execute the required atomic skills. We discuss these failure cases in Appendix D.3. 5. Conclusion We presented A MF E, WAM that repurposes pretrained video diffusion models as predictive visual encoders through future representation distillation. By distilling video priors from the intermediate representations of frozen video diffusion model with access to future frames, A MF learns to predict future visual representations that guide action prediction without generating future videos. Experiments demonstrate strong manipulation performance in both simulation and the real world, with significant inference speedup over video-generating WAM. A MF benefits from larger video backbone and more video data, and enables task transfer from video demonstrations. These findings highlight predictive representation learning as an effective way to translate pretrained video knowledge into robot control and expand robot capabilities through video-based learning.

sections.content: A. Model architecture details A.1. Video backbone adaptation We fine-tune the pretrained video diffusion backbone [25] on robot videos to adapt it to the robotics domain and our multi-view packing format. Due to computational constraints, we do not use additional external video data in this stage. The adapted checkpoint initializes both the teacher and student of the same architecture. During visual-encoder training, the teacher remains frozen with bidirectional video attention and text cross-attention on all frames. The student uses the modifications below. The VAE and text encoder remain frozen throughout adaptation and visual-encoder training. A.2. Visual encoder Video DiT Following Fast-WAM [30], we prevent current observation tokens from attending to future latent tokens. To encourage the current observation representation to capture planning-related information, we restrict each future latent frame to attend only to the current observation frame and itself, and disable text cross-attention for future latent tokens. Spatial attention is preserved within each frame. Unlike Wan2.2-TI2V-5B, Wan2.2-I2V-A14B uses separate image-conditioning mechanism, where sequence consisting of the first image followed by zero-valued frames is VAE-encoded. To adopt the same first-frame conditioning strategy as TI2V-5B, we replace the first frame of the noisy video-latent stream with its clean latent and assign it timestep zero. Projector To match the teachers spatiotemporal token sequence length, the projector expands 𝑁 current observation tokens to 𝐹𝑁 tokens, where 𝐹 is the number of latent frames in the teachers future representation. The student and teacher use the same spatial token grid. The student tokens are replicated 𝐹 times and augmented with learned frame embeddings, then fed into two-layer decoder as queries. Each decoder layer applies self-attention, cross-attention to the original student tokens, and 1024 4096 1024 GELU MLP, with pre-normalization and residual connections in each sublayer. Student and teacher features are extracted after complete Transformer blocks 𝑖 and 𝑗, respectively. To supervise future positions only, we exclude current observation tokens from both projector outputs and teacher targets. The loss is the mean cosine distance over the remaining token pairs after non-affine feature-wise LayerNorm (𝜖 = 106). A.3. Action readout module During action-module training, the visual encoder is frozen. The readout and conditioning layers are trained from scratch. The readout receives current observation tokens from encoder block 𝑘, independently selected from distillation block 𝑖, without passing through the alignment projector. To obtain fixed-length visual context for the action decoder, we use 64 learned queries updated by two blocks. Each decoder layer applies self-attention, cross-attention to the projected visual tokens, and 1024 4096 1024 GELU MLP. All sublayers use pre-normalization and residual connections. Output LayerNorm is followed by separate 1024 1024 conditioning projection and affine LayerNorm. These visual tokens are appended to the projected instruction tokens as decoder cross-attention context. A.4. A.5. Action decoder The decoder uses 30 DiT blocks, hidden width 1024, feed-forward width 4096, and 24 attention heads of dimension 128, totaling approximately 1B parameters. Each block contains bidirectional self-attention over state/history/action tokens and cross-attention to instruction and visual context from the action readout module. Self-attention uses one-dimensional rotary position embeddings and padding masks. 256-dimensional sinusoidal timestep embedding and an MLP provide block modulation. final linear layer predicts the flow-matching velocity in action space, and prefix outputs are discarded, and loss is computed only at valid future-action positions. For DROID, we include history of the previous 8 actions to address unintended gripper reopening during closed-loop execution. History uses the same linear encoder as noisy actions. The input order is current state, action history, then noisy future actions. Missing history entries are masked, and the entire history is independently dropped with probability 0.2 during training. State and history remain noise-free, with fixed timestep corresponding to 𝜎 = 103. A.6. Training and inference algorithms Algorithms 1 and 2 summarize training and synchronous closed-loop inference. We write 𝒙 for VAEencoded video latents, with superscripts 0 and + selecting current observation and future positions. Video-model calls also include the Wan-A14B image-conditioning channels when applicable. sg denotes stop-gradient, LN is non-affine token-wise LayerNorm, and sim is mean cosine similarity after this normalization. States and actions are normalized. 𝒔 denotes optional action history, used only for DROID. Here, 𝑝train samples 𝑡 = 5𝑟/(1 + 4𝑟) with 𝑟 (0, 1), and 𝑤(𝑡) is the native schedulers timestep weight. Losses are averaged over the batch. MSE𝑚 excludes padded action positions. The implemented cosine loss 1 sim differs from sim only by an additive constant. Teacher conditioning keeps the first frame clean for 5B, and Wan-A14B retains noised first frame in the video stream and separate clean image conditioning. 17 B. Implementation details B.1. Baselines For simulation benchmarks, we use reported baseline scores except for Fast-WAM on RoboCasa-Kitchen, which we train and evaluate ourselves. Fast-WAM [30] For RoboCasa-Kitchen, we train Fast-WAM 5B using the official implementation with learning rate 104 for 20 epochs and global batch size 128. The 14B baseline uses the Wan2.2-A14B high-noise expert with global batch size 32. We modify the conditioning on the current observation frame to match that of our method. B.2. A MF We use AdamW with learning rate of 104 for both training stages. For LIBERO and Robocasa models, we use rank-128 LoRA to train the visual encoders initialized from the video diffusion models. For the 14B DROID model, we fully train the weights without using LoRA. Input resolutions are 224 448 for LIBERO, 352 352 for RoboCasa, and 352 640 for DROID. We set the teacher noise level to 𝑡𝑑 = 0.7 for simulation benchmarks and 0.8 for DROID. The layer indices used for our distillation loss and action readout are fixed for each backbone size across all datasets and tasks. For the 5B backbone, we extract student features for distillation at 𝑖 = 25 and features for action readout at 𝑘 = 19. For the 14B backbone, we use 𝑖 = 𝑗 = 𝑘 = 31. All indices are zero-based, and features are extracted after the corresponding complete Transformer block. For LIBERO, we use global batch sizes of 128 and 64 in stages 1 and 2, respectively. Stage 1 runs for 40 epochs, and stage 2 for 10 epochs. For RoboCasa 5B, we use global batch sizes of 64 and 256 in stages 1 and 2, respectively, for four and 20 epochs. For RoboCasa 14B, we use global batch sizes of 32 and 512 in stages 1 and 2, respectively. Stage 1 runs for 10 epochs on RoboCasa-only videos or two epochs with additional videos, and stage 2 runs for 20 epochs. For DROID, we fully train the visual encoder in stage 1 without LoRA. We use global batch sizes of 64 and 4,096 in stages 1 and 2, respectively, for 6 and 16 epochs. Training across both stages took approximately one week on 16 NVIDIA H200 GPUs. For ABC-130k [1], we train our model on subset of approximately 100 hours from the full 3,500-hour dataset due to computational constraints. The subset is selected to cover diverse tasks and operators. We use the 14B backbone with an input resolution of 432 384. For the bimanual setup, the overhead view occupies the upper two-thirds of the input, while the left and right wrist views are arranged side by side in the lower third. We follow the DROID 14B optimization settings, including global batch sizes of 64 and 4,096 for stages 1 and 2, respectively. Inference The visual encoder runs once at timestep zero, without video denoising or classifier-free guidance (CFG). Actions are initialized from Gaussian noise and sampled with 10 Euler steps for LIBERO and RoboCasa, and 16 steps for DROID, using flow-matching schedule with shift 5. Action sampling also omits CFG, requiring one conditional decoder evaluation per step. From each 32-action chunk, we execute 10 actions in LIBERO, 32 in RoboCasa, and 24 in DROID before replanning. C. Experimental details C.1. Simulation benchmarks LIBERO We use the same multi-view frame packing setup as in the official Fast-WAM implementation. We report the average success rate across the four LIBERO suites, evaluated over total of 2,000 trials covering 40 tasks with different random seeds. The baseline results are taken from Yuan et al. [30]. Robocasa-Kitchen We use the Cosmos Policy [15] dataset with 50 human-teleoperated demonstrations per task. We train and evaluate A MF and Fast-WAM on this benchmark and use reported scores for the remaining baselines. Connection to prior works Comparison with Fast-WAM [30] Fast-WAM uses pretrained video diffusion backbone for direct action prediction, retaining video co-training but omitting future-video denoising at deployment. The key difference is that A MF directly supervises the policy features with future representation distillation in addition to the video generative objective. In our RoboCasa-Kitchen experiments  (Table 2)  , Fast-WAM substantially trails the video-generating WAM baseline and shows little improvement from 5B to 14B backbone (44.4% to 44.7%). These results suggest that generative supervision through shared weights alone does not ensure that larger VDM provides more useful predictive features for control. A MF supports learning and transfer from videos without action labels, while achieving performance and generalization competitive with video-generating WAMs at substantially lower inference latency. Knowledge Insulation [8] Freezing the visual encoder in stage 2 prevents gradients from the action DiT from updating the video backbone. Knowledge Insulation and LAP [31] similarly block gradients from the action expert while training VLM representations through FAST-token prediction and language-action prediction, respectively. Our method applies similar separation to VDM, using the native video generative objective and future representation distillation to shape the visual features. Their concurrent training also suggests an alternative to our two-stage procedure: jointly training the encoder and action module with their respective objectives, while blocking action-module gradients from the encoder. We leave this variant to future work, as we have not evaluated it due to computational constraints. E.2. Limitations Although A MF uses video-model priors to predict actions directly like VLAs, achieving lower latency than video-generating WAMs, several limitations remain. Scaling with embodied pretraining. We demonstrate that 14B video backbone trained on DROID without embodied pretraining can outperform existing VLA and WAM baselines. Although the RoboCasa results in Table 2 suggest that additional video data could further improve performance, 22 we did not evaluate this extension on DROID due to computational constraints. Scaling to larger backbones, datasets, and embodiments remains an important direction for future work. Training complexity. Our pipeline separates backbone adaptation, predictive representation learning, and action learning. Simplifying these stages and exploring joint training of the visual encoder and action module remain directions for future work.
